title: How to write with AI and still sound like you
description: Research a subject properly, draft in your own voice, and adapt finished work across the channels you publish on.
introduction: You can always tell. The rhythm flattens, every paragraph resolves into the same tidy takeaway, and nothing in it could only have been written by one person. Which is why most writers who try it end up rewriting the draft completely and deciding the whole thing costs more than it saves.

That happens because generating prose is the one part of writing you shouldn't outsource. The parts worth handing over are the ones that eat the day: learning a subject well enough to say something true about it, finding the sources that hold up, and turning one finished piece into the five formats it owes. Strawberry works in the browser, so it can research a subject across real sites and logged-in tools, keep the link and date beside every claim, and learn your voice from work you have already published.

sections.title: What Strawberry can help you do

items.title: Know the subject
items.description: Learn a topic well enough to have a position, with sources that hold up.

items.title: Sound like yourself
items.description: Teach your companion your voice from work you have already published.

items.title: Make one piece go further
items.description: Adapt finished work into the other formats it owes without flattening it.

items.title: Decide what is next
items.description: Plan what to publish based on what worked and what you have not covered.

blocks.text: Not sure where to start? Tell your companion what you are working on and it can suggest the most useful first step.

skill.context: Help me work out where to start with the piece I am writing.

blocks.text: Writing that falls flat usually fails on substance rather than style. The author read three summaries, found nothing anyone else had missed, and wrote around the gap.

Strawberry can follow a subject past the first page of results, into documentation, filings, forums, archives, and the logged-in tools you already pay for. What you want out of that isn't coverage. It's the one detail worth building a piece around: the contradiction, the number smaller than everyone assumes, the thing practitioners say that the marketing doesn't.

items.title: Map an unfamiliar subject
items.text: See the main positions, who is worth reading, and which arguments are already exhausted.

skill.context: Map this topic so I understand the landscape before I write.

items.title: Research one organization
items.text: Separate what a company claims about itself from what is independently supported.

skill.context: Research this organization for the piece I am writing.

blocks.text: Give your companion two or three pieces you're happy with and it works from your actual voice. Your sentence rhythm, how much you qualify, whether you use humor, what you refuse to say. That's a different exercise from asking for a tone, and it's the difference between a draft you edit and a draft you bin.
It won't invent a quotation, a statistic, or a person to make a paragraph land. For anything going out under your own name, that matters more than any amount of fluency.

A finished piece usually owes several more: the newsletter version, the thread, the talk, the client-facing one-pager. Most of that work is mechanical, which is exactly why it gets done badly or not at all.

items.title: Adapt it across channels
items.text: Rework the same argument for the places you actually publish, without compressing it into something generic.

skill.context: Adapt this finished piece for the other channels I publish on.

items.title: Turn it into something presented
items.text: Move from a written argument to a talk or deck when the audience needs to watch rather than read.

skill.context: Turn this piece into a presentation.

blocks.text: The hardest editorial question is what to make next, and most people answer it from whatever they read that morning. A plan built from what's actually worked, and what you haven't covered yet, beats that.

items.context: Help me plan what to publish next.

blocks.text: Voice is the part worth protecting. Once your companion has it right, that calibration can be saved along with the sources you trust, the structure you tend to use, and how blunt you want the feedback. The next piece starts from there rather than from a cold start.
If you write with an editor, a team, or a client, the accepted voice and standards can be shared so the work stays recognisably yours no matter who briefs it.

items.context: Turn our accepted voice and standards into something the team can reuse.
